name: Velocity
description: Speed with direction—how fast something is moving AND which way

content.overview: Ever notice how "60 km/h" doesn't tell you the whole story? Sixty km/h toward home and sixty km/h away from home are pretty different situations! That extra bit of info - which way you're going - is what turns plain old speed into velocity. Velocity = speed + direction, and once you see it that way, it just clicks.
content.explanation:
Here's the formula: velocity = displacement ÷ time. Nothing scary about it - you're just dividing, same as with speed. The difference is what you divide.

Velocity is a VECTOR, which just means it comes with a direction attached. Speed only tells you "how fast." Velocity tells you "how fast, and which way." Think about giving someone directions - saying "go 5 km" is way less useful than "go 5 km north." That's basically the speed-vs-velocity difference in a nutshell.

**Velocity vs Speed, side by side:**
- Speed: "60 km/h" (just a number - a scalar)
- Velocity: "60 km/h north" (number + direction - a vector)

**Average vs instantaneous - what's the difference?**
- Average velocity = your overall displacement ÷ the total time (the big-picture view)
- Instantaneous velocity = your velocity at one single moment (what your speedometer-plus-compass would show right now) {{viz:anim-01}}

**Let's drive through an example:**
Say you drive 100 km north in 2 hours.
- Average speed = 100 km ÷ 2 h = 50 km/h
- Average velocity = 100 km north ÷ 2 h = 50 km/h north

Same number, but velocity gives you the bonus direction. {{viz:chart-01}}

**Now here's a fun twist - jogging example:**
You jog 100 m east, then jog 100 m back west to where you started.
- Distance = 200 m (your legs definitely worked for it, so speed is a real, positive number)
- Displacement = 0 m, since you ended up right back where you began
- So your average velocity = 0 m/s, even though you were clearly moving the whole time!

Weird, right? But it makes sense once you remember velocity only cares about your net change in position, not how much ground you actually covered.

And yes, velocity can be negative - that's not an error, it just means "moving the opposite way" (backward, downward, west, whatever you defined as negative). The sign is doing real work here, not just decoration. {{viz:diagram-01}}

**Why physics is obsessed with velocity:** once you start looking at forces and acceleration, direction becomes everything. A car speeding up and a car turning a corner at constant speed are both "accelerating" in physics-speak, because velocity is changing - and that only makes sense once direction is in the picture. {{viz:simulation-01}}
keyPoints: Velocity = displacement ÷ time - same idea as speed, but direction comes along for the ride
It's a vector: magnitude (how fast) + direction (which way)
Speed is just |velocity| - the direction stripped away
Velocity can be negative - that just means moving the other way
Physics leans on velocity way more than speed, because direction matters for forces and acceleration
content.whyItMatters: Velocity is one of the most useful ideas you'll carry through mechanics. It doesn't just tell you how fast something's moving - it tells you where it's heading, which turns out to be essential once you start dealing with forces and acceleration. Get comfortable with velocity now, and a lot of what comes next will feel a lot less mysterious.
